The text correctly translates Paul’s words as directly ascribing deity to Christ. See theological note “The Deity of Christ” on p. 1851.

**9:6 word of God.** His promise and plan to be the God of Abraham’s seed (Gen. 17:7, 8). In the OT era, natural descent did not automatically guarantee inheritance of the promise. God chose who would inherit it. As Paul goes on to show, this principle is evident in the families of Abraham and Isaac.

The biblical narrative of Abraham shows that not all biological descendants of the patriarch are chosen by God for His covenant favor. Although Ishmael was Abraham’s child “of the flesh” (v. 8), that did not make him Abraham’s “offspring” from the standpoint of God’s covenant promise of blessing. Rather, Isaac was specifically identified as the heir to and through whom God’s covenant favor would be extended, as demonstrated in Gen. 21:12 (see Gal. 4:21–31).

The case of Jacob and Esau clinches the argument in three ways: (a) because they were twins, they were as nearly equal in nature as possible; (b) because the purpose of God reversed even the small distinction that did exist, by causing the older brother to serve the younger (inverting cultural expectations, Gen. 48:13–20; 49:3, 4; Deut. 21:15–17); (c) because the purpose of God was stated before they were born (and therefore was not dependent on their actions). Election is not based on foreseen actions, deeds, or faith. Rather, it is based on God’s sovereign predestinating grace.

verse_quote: Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.
note: This distinguishing purpose of God in election (v. 11) is further confirmed by the words of Mal. 1:2, 3, which explain God’s love to Israel as rooted in His free choice of Jacob rather than Esau. “Hated” here cannot be reduced to “loved less,” as the context of Mal. 1:3, 4 makes clear. It must carry the sense of rejection and antipathy.

Cf. 8:31. Paul recognizes that his previous statement cannot be allowed to pass without further comment. Could the distinguishing sovereign purpose of God throw into jeopardy His attribute of perfect righteousness? The idea is clearly unthinkable: “By no means!” (6:2, 15; 7:7). Paul explains by citing two biblical texts (Ex. 33:19; 9:16) in vv. 15, 17, from which he concludes that God is righteous in showing mercy to some while He hardens the hearts of others. When God shows mercy, it is not a person receiving a reward earned by one’s own efforts but God’s sovereign free grace extended to undeserving persons who are morally incapable of any acceptable effort (1:18–3:20). God owes mercy to none, so there is no injustice when mercy is not shown. Mercy is a divine prerogative; it rests on God’s good pleasure. When God “hardens” Pharaoh’s heart (v. 18), He does not create fresh evil in it, but gives Pharaoh over to his already evil desires as an act of judgment (cf. 1:26, 28), resulting eventually in God’s display of “power” (v. 22) in the destruction of Pharaoh’s army (Ex. 14:17, 18, 23–28).

verse_quote: not on human will or exertion, but on God.
note: God’s sovereign bestowal of mercy on undeserving sinners, chosen by grace, silences all human boasting (4:2; 1 Cor. 1:29; Eph. 2:8, 9) and every human charge of injustice against God.
It was God who thus spoke to Pharaoh through Moses (Ex. 9:16), but for Paul the words of Scripture and the voice and authority of God are one.
See theological note “Predestination and Reprobation” on the next page.

verse_quote: Why does he still find fault.
note: By what right can God lay the blame for their sins on those He has hardened against Himself? Paul answers partially in terms of human experience (vv. 20, 21). It is unreasonable and irreverent for anyone to question the rightness of God’s ways. Potters have every right to do as they please with the clay (Is. 64:8). All people belong to “the same lump” (cf. vv. 10–13) of fallen humanity in Adam (5:12–14); all actively sin even before God judicially hardens them in their commitment to ungodliness and unrighteousness (1:18–28). That God should show mercy to any from the Adamic lump and create vessels of honor from it is the kindness of grace; that others should become vessels for lesser use is a matter of His sovereign prerogative and is itself a display of perfect justice toward them.

See theological note “Predestination” on p. 1650. Paul does not elaborate on the preparation in view. The addition of “beforehand” in connection with the vessels of mercy may be pointing to the mercy that originates in God’s good pleasure from eternity (8:29, 30). The distinction between elect and reprobate does not lie in anything in themselves (all deserve wrath), but exclusively in the will of God. Within that context, however, the objects prepared for destruction experience wrath that is the only possible and just reward for sin.

Extending his discussion of God’s mysterious and unmerited mercy, Paul uses OT Scriptures to make two further points: (1) Not only are many biological descendants of Abraham excluded from the elect who receive mercy, but also the elect includes Gentiles who believe, who once were not God’s people. (2) Despite Israel’s widespread unbelief, God is preserving a remnant for salvation among ethnic Israel.

Hos. 1:10 originally applied to the northern tribes, who had forfeited their covenant status through apostasy and idolatry. Paul sees in the promise that God will restore such rebels, bringing them back into covenant favor and calling them “sons of the living God,” a sign of the breadth of God’s electing love, which now includes even Gentiles with pagan pasts, who were never “my people” before Christ. Gentiles can fulfill this prophecy through faith in and union with the true Israelite, Jesus., 26

See v. 14. Having accounted for Jewish unbelief in terms of divine sovereignty, Paul now diagnoses that unbelief as due to a fatal prior commitment to a false way of righteousness. Divine sovereignty and the guilt of human willfulness are for Paul two aspects of reality. By God’s grace and sovereignty, Gentiles who did not seek God’s righteousness have now received it through faith in Christ, but Israel as a people has failed to receive it because the nation has sought it by a legal means in which it could not be found, since it subtly replaces trust in God with self-reliance. To those Jews seeking to establish their own righteousness on the basis of the law, Christ has been a stumbling stone (the image is from Is. 8:14; 28:16) over which they have fallen (vv. 32, 33; 1 Pet. 2:8; cf. Luke 2:34).

verse_quote: a law that would lead to righteousness.
note: Paul probably has the Mosaic law in view again, and the Jews’ expectation that their adherence to it can secure God’s favor. The Jews’ mistake lies not in what they have pursued (righteousness, God’s vindicating verdict), but in their manner of pursuing it (“not ... by faith, but ... works,” v. 32).

A heartfelt appeal to the sympathy of his fellow Christians, the pathos of which is underlined by his recent reference to his relatives in the flesh (9:3, text note).

**that they may be saved.** Paul’s concern in ch. 9 is with the salvation of the Jews, not merely with their role in redemptive history. He hopes that the gospel’s fruitfulness among the Gentiles will make his Jewish kinsmen envious of such grace, and so draw them in faith to Jesus the Messiah (vv. 19, 20; 11:11–14).
From personal experience, Paul speaks here as to both the reality of the zeal and its wrongheaded and wrong-hearted character (Phil. 3:4–6).

verse_quote: being ignorant of the righteousness of God.
note:
Paul contrasts, on the one hand, the divinely established righteousness provided through Christ and, on the other, a person’s efforts to establish one’s own righteousness through scrupulous law observance. See theological note “Faith and Works” on p. 2231.

**establish.** Covenant language (Gen. 6:18; 17:7). Even in the context of the covenant God made with them, they have perverted His grace by seeing it as dependent on their own law-keeping.

verse_quote: Christ is the end of the law.
note: One interpretation is that Christ is the goal or purpose of the law (Gal. 3:24). A second interpretation is that for believers, Christ terminates any pursuit of the law in order to establish their own righteousness by it. These two views are not mutually exclusive and together make good sense of Paul’s argument in Romans and in Galatians (cf. Gal. 3:15–29).

verse_quote: the righteousness that is based on the law.
note: Paul’s quotation from Lev. 18:5 is set originally in the context of God’s redemptive grace requiring a person’s responsive obedience (Lev. 18:2; cf. Ex. 20:1–17); to those who reject that grace, however, Paul points to Lev. 18:5 as a statement that only perfect law-keeping can merit eternal life if people choose to try and merit eternal life by keeping the law. This is an impossible condition for sinners to meet (cf. 9:31, 32).

The law of Moses exhibits God’s salvation as secured not by humanity’s strenuous efforts, but by divine grace bringing it near. In particular, Deut. 30 sets this salvation in the context of an anticipated return from the judgment of exile (Deut. 30:1–6). Paul sees this fulfilled in the new covenant in Christ (Jer. 31:31–34, cf. 2 Cor. 3:7–18). Thus, Christ is the end of any pursuit of the law for the righteousness of justification. To seek a self-established righteousness now is the equivalent of attempting to do what God alone can do and has done in Christ’s incarnation and resurrection. By contrast with all human efforts, God has brought near the word of salvation, and with it salvation itself. See theological note “Special Revelation and the Bible” on p. 142.

In the parallelism of v. 10, Paul reverses the order of verbs in v. 9 and thereby indicates that heart-belief and mouth-confession belong together for justification (“righteousness”) and salvation., 10

Paul returns to his earlier theme that just as there is no distinction between Jews and Gentiles with respect to universal sinfulness, so God makes no distinction in bestowing salvation by grace to believers of all races and backgrounds (3:22–24, 29, 30; cf. Gal. 3:28). This is confirmed not only by the unity and universal kindness of God (v. 12) but specifically again by the teaching of the OT in Joel 2:32 (cited in v. 13), the statement fulfilled so dramatically at Pentecost (Acts 2:21).

This prophecy about Israel’s salvation can also be fulfilled in Gentiles because when they identify with and believe in Jesus, the true Israel, they become true Israel (a point made in Rom. 11:23, 24, where believing Jews and Gentiles make up the one people of God), and so can be seen naturally to fulfill this prophecy about Israel. See Acts 2:17–21 and 10:44–48 for the same rationale as to why Gentiles can fulfill the same Joel 2 prophecy.

An analysis of what is involved when anyone calls on the name of the Lord in order to be saved.

**10:14 him in whom.** Lit. “Him whom.” This statement implies that for Paul, Christ Himself is the one true preacher of the gospel, whose voice calls His elect through His servants’ gospel proclamation (cf. Eph. 2:17; John 10:16). The ministry of preaching Christ is therefore one of great honor; hence the quotation from Is. 52:7 (2 Cor. 5:18–20).

verse_quote: Their voice has gone out to all the earth.
note: The immediate context of the citation from Ps. 19:4 is that of God’s general revelation (Ps. 19:1–3). Paul’s use of it to prove from Scripture that Israel has heard the message of God implies that his quotation of this section of the psalm carries with it the teaching of the entire psalm, which speaks of both general revelation in nature and special revelation in His Word. The latter takes place in the context of the former. The underlying logic may be: If those without special revelation have “heard” the message of God’s glory in creation, how much more have those who possess special revelation heard that message? Moreover, the special revelation of saving grace in Christ is now spreading over the earth, to all the nations, until its message envelops the world, eventually becoming coextensive with the created order’s display of God’s eternal power and divine nature (1:20).

The failure of the Jews cannot be excused because they did not hear the message or because they could not understand it. Moses and Isaiah contrast God’s own people with those who lack understanding (Deut. 32:21) and with those who were not God-seekers but who were brought to know Him (Is. 65:1). Each major section of the Hebrew canon (Law, v. 19; Prophets, v. 20; Writings, v. 18) testifies to Israel’s culpability.

Paul now pointedly asks whether God has rejected His people. The apostle himself is evidence that God has not fully and finally rejected the people on whom He set His love. Just as a believing remnant could be found in Israel in Elijah’s day, so there continues to be a remnant formed by God’s grace. By grace, the elect obtain the salvation they seek. The rest are hardened.

**11:1 has God rejected.** The verb conveys the sense of vigorously pushing away from Himself. The form of the question in Greek anticipates a negative answer.

**I myself am an Israelite.** See Phil. 3:5, 6. Paul’s impeccable lineage is traced back to Abraham, the great patriarch, but also to Benjamin, the only son of Jacob to be born in Canaan. It was the tribe of Saul, the first king, the tribe in whose territory Jerusalem and the temple were located, and one of two tribes (with Judah) that remained loyal to the Davidic dynasty upon the division of the kingdom (1 Kin. 12:20–24).

Paul hints that God’s special love and gracious choice (cf. 8:29; Amos 3:2) of Israel makes it unthinkable that He should completely reject them as a people, even though many of them have now rejected Him by rejecting Christ.

In Elijah’s time, there was wholesale apostasy, and yet the presence of a remnant of the faithful indicated that God had not fully and finally rejected His people. Paul’s thinking about the remnant is rooted in the teaching of Isaiah, whose son Shear-jashub’s name means “a remnant shall return” (Is. 7:3 and text note; cf. Is. 1:9; 6:13; 10:20–22; 11:11–16; Rom. 9:27).

verse_quote: But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works.
note: Again the way of grace is contrasted with works of the law (3:20, 27, 28; 4:2, 6; 9:12, 32).

The passages cited (Deut. 29:4; Is. 29:10; Ps. 69:22, 23), representing each major section of the canon of OT Scripture, describe a biblical pattern of divine activity in the judicial hardening of hearts (cf. 9:15–18; 1:24, 26)—a pattern Paul sees repeated in his own day.

Paul has thus far argued that the rejection of the Jewish people is not total. Now, he argues that it is not final. Just as the rejection of Christ among the Jews has led to the acceptance of the gospel among the Gentiles, so God means to use the Gentiles to provoke the Jews to envy the Gentiles’ blessings, leading to their salvation and correspondingly greater riches.

**11:11 did they stumble in order that they might fall.** Once again the form of Paul’s question anticipates (and receives) a negative answer. The Jews’ rejection of Christ is not irreversible. Paul sees a divine pattern and purpose behind the unbelief of which the Jews are guilty. The pattern of his thought in v. 11, therefore, is as follows: (a) the transgression of the Jews has led to the justification of the Gentiles; (b) the salvation of the Gentiles will cause the Jews to envy; (c) the envy of the Jews will draw them to the same salvation as the Gentiles.

In the context of Paul’s argument, “full inclusion” here can only signify their reception of Christ and their restoration to God. The more difficult question is whether the term “full” points to the remnant or to the nation of Israel as a whole. The second seems to better fit the general direction of the passage, which suggests that there will be a large increase in the number of Jewish people who recognize Jesus as the Messiah just before the return of Christ to judge the living and the dead (vv. 25–32).

verse_quote: a I am speaking to you Gentiles.
note:
Why he singles out the Gentiles in the Roman church is made clear in vv. 17–24.

**11:13b, 14 apostle to the Gentiles ... to make my fellow Jews jealous.** Paul here provides a unique insight into his thinking about his ministry to the Gentiles: the apostle’s ministry also has his own Jewish people in view, in terms of 10:19 and 11:11 (cf. Acts 9:15; Eph. 3:1; Gal. 2:8). His work among the Gentiles has as its goal the salvation of the Jews as well., 14

This phrase may simply denote unprecedented blessing. Although the wording is slightly different from Paul’s normal usage (“resurrection from the dead,” 1:4; cf. 1 Cor. 15:12, 13, 21, 42), the phrase may refer to the general resurrection of the last day or it may refer to the inaugurated spiritual resurrection that occurs when a Jew comes to faith during the time between Christ’s comings. Since “life from the dead” is in parallel with “reconciliation” at the beginning of the verse, this latter view may be best.
Paul applies spiritually the principle that the firstfruits serve as the pledge of the final harvest (cf. Num. 15:17–21).

verse_quote: a wild olive shoot ... grafted in.
note: See Jer. 11:16; Hos. 14:6 for Israel as an olive tree. It does not seem that it was a first-century practice to graft wild olive shoots into cultivated trees to bring fresh vitality to them. Paul’s words, however, probably intentionally stretch beyond strict horticulture. Gentiles have been grafted into the people of God “contrary to nature” (v. 24).

Because their salvation is entirely by grace, Gentiles have no cause for boasting or despising Jewish unbelievers. Such Gentile arrogance in relation to these Jews would simply mirror the same spiritual pride that has led to the Jews’ hardening (2:17).

While the rejoinder to Paul in v. 19 is formally true, the breaking off of the Jewish branches was an act of righteous judgment on unbelief, and the ingrafting of the Gentiles is through faith and therefore a matter of grace. Their ingrafting (v. 19) is not therefore based on any superior quality in the Gentiles.

**fear.** Tender-spirited awe, not arrogance, is the appropriate response to God’s grace.

verse_quote: Note then the kindness and the severity of God.
note: See theological note “Predestination” on p. 1650. Gentile believers are urged to take seriously the revelation of God’s character in these events of providence. God’s kindness bears fruit only when His people continue in it (2:4).

The cutting off of Israel is because of unbelief, and not because the Gentiles are inherently better qualified for life in the olive tree. Moreover, if unbelieving Jews come to believe the gospel, they will be “grafted back,” even as believing Gentiles have been “grafted, contrary to nature.”, 24

Paul’s close reasoning here has been understood in three major ways: (a) He is showing how God saves all of His elect people (“all Israel” in v. 26 being taken as basically synonymous with the church, that is, spiritual Israel, composed of the elect from every nation). (b) He is showing how God saves all the elect of (ethnic) Israel who are to be saved. (c) He is showing how God will, in the future, bring such widespread salvation to the Jewish people that, in an obvious general sense, it can be said that “all Israel will be saved” (v. 26). While not without difficulties, some form of this last view seems most likely for the following reasons. First, hints of it seem to appear already in vv. 11, 12, 15, 16, 24. Second, v. 25 suggests that an end to the partial hardening of Israel is in view. Third, “Israel” in v. 26 is not naturally interpreted as signifying a different entity from the Israel in view in vv. 1–24 and vv. 28–31, where national Israel (not spiritual Israel) is in view. Fourth, “mystery”—a matter known only through divine revelation—in v. 25 would seem inappropriate and exaggerated if Paul’s teaching were simply that all elect Jews will be saved. Finally, this view accords well with the quotations in vv. 26, 27 from Is. 59:20, 21; 27:9; Jer. 31:33, 34, which appear to speak of a comprehensive banishment of that sin that has been the cause of Israel’s alienation from God.

**11:25 mystery.** In Paul, and in Jewish thought generally, a divine secret that has now been revealed (16:25, 26; Eph. 3:3–9). Some interpreters conclude that what immediately follows constitutes the mystery (probably the widespread conversion of the Jews). Others hold that the mystery is the pattern of God’s working in the Jew-Gentile interrelationship referred to in v. 11. The mystery may simply be the fact that, though it was evident that only a remnant of Israel would be saved in the latter days, it was not as clear according to OT prophecy that a majority of those saved would be Gentiles in comparison to only a remnant of saved Jews.

**fullness.** The term may be taken to have a specifically numerical connotation. The ESV translates the same Gk. word as “full inclusion” in 11:12.

**has come in.** An expression used infrequently by Paul, but commonly found in the Gospels to describe entrance into life or the kingdom of God (e.g., Mark 9:47).

A critical expression at this point in Paul’s argument, and one whose meaning is much debated. It could mean “all (spiritual) Israel,” that is, all elect persons, both Jew and Gentile. Alternately, it may mean “all” Israel in the sense of a remnant of “all Jews destined to be saved throughout history.” Or, as also noted above, it may point to a time when a mass conversion of ethnic Jews to Christ will occur. The use of the term “Israel” to refer to the biological descendants of the patriarchs throughout Paul’s discussion favors one of the last two interpretations. See note on 11:25–32, points (a), (b), and (c). The exegesis of “all Israel” will depend on the interpretation and weighing of other factors in the passage.

**The Deliverer will come from Zion.** The quotation is from Ps. 14:7; Is. 27:9; 59:20, 21. Possibly Paul quotes this text in reference to the return of Christ from the heavenly Zion at the end of the age. Alternatively, it may refer to Christ’s first coming, when “ungodliness” was banished by Jesus from those Jews who believed in Him, at which time Christ executed the new “covenant” (likely referred to at the end of v. 27, “when I [God] take away their sins”). The latter view accords most with the book of Hebrews, which sees Jesus’ first coming to be the decisive time when He established the new covenant (e.g., Heb. 8:6–13; 10:1–16).

The presence of a believing remnant in Paul’s day (including Paul himself) and the promise of God’s ingathering of many more Jews to faith in Jesus the Messiah show that God has not revoked His calling and gifts to His ancient covenant people (9:6; 11:1, 2).

Paul’s argument concludes in a manner parallel to 3:19–21, stressing that Jew and Gentile are united in two things: the disobedience of sin, and the offer to them of the mercy of God. The wisdom and sovereignty of God’s grace are demonstrated in the way in which His purposes are fulfilled: the disobedience of the Jew leads to the Gentiles’ receiving God’s mercy; the mercy of God to the Gentiles leads to the reception of mercy by the Jews. There is no difference—all (Jew and Gentile alike) have sinned (3:23), and God has mercy on both (1:16).

Having drawn together the various strands of his argument, Paul now responds in lyrical fashion with a song of praise that reaches heights that correspond to the depth of concern he sounded in 9:2, 3. God’s dealings with Jew and Gentile display a cross-section of His majesty in which His sovereign will (“from him”), His sovereign activity (“through him”) and His sovereign glory (“to him”) are richly displayed (v. 36).

The doxology at the end of ch. 11 and the nature of the opening verses of ch. 12 signal a new stage in Paul’s exposition. Paul’s “appeal” or exhortation, founded (“therefore”) on God’s mercies, turns the corner from his exposition of God’s saving work to the response that God’s grace should elicit from believers. From now until the conclusion of the letter, he focuses on applying his teaching to Christians’ behavior and relationships.

**mercies of God.** Paul can summarize the teaching of Rom. 3–11 in terms of God’s undeserved favor to needy sinners. The biblical doctrine of grace leads to a life motivated by gratitude.

**present your bodies as a living sacrifice.** Jew and Gentile now belong together as the people of God for whom the final blood sacrifice has been made (3:25). The sacrifice that remains is that of thankful response (cf. 6:17). “Bodies” means whole persons as embodied individuals (6:12, 13, 19; 8:13). Paul will use this sacrificial imagery in 15:16 to portray his “priestly” ministry as an apostle, bringing believing Gentiles as offerings in worship of his Lord (see Phil. 2:17).

**spiritual worship.** The worship that is appropriate for redeemed creatures to offer (see text note, giving the alternative “rational service”). The Gk. term rendered “spiritual” here does not allude to God’s Spirit (unlike, for instance, 1 Cor. 12:1), but distinguishes Christians’ worship from the animal sacrifices of OT worship. Nevertheless, our worship is now undertaken by the power of the Holy Spirit (15:16).

verse_quote: Do not be conformed ... be transformed by the renewal of your mind.
note: Formerly, Christians were “futile in their thinking” (1:21). But now, the Christian’s mindset is to be determined and reshaped by knowledge of the gospel, by the power of the Spirit, and by the concerns of the age to come (8:5–9; 13:11–14), rather than by the passing fashion of this age (2 Cor. 4:18; 1 John 2:17). Only by such sanctifying renewal is the Christian made sufficiently sensitive to “discern” the behavior that God’s revealed will requires in each situation.

verse_quote: by the grace given to me.
note: Paul’s ministry exists only because of grace (1:5), as do spiritual gifts (Gk. _charismata,_ v. 6). Realistic assessment of one’s gift (“think with sober judgment”) is essential, and involves a recognition of one’s “measure of faith,” that is, knowing to what extent one has the faith suited for exercising particular gifts (v. 6). The faith by which we are justified is a separate question.

As in 1 Cor. 12, Paul makes use of the analogy of the body and its various parts to illustrate the nature of the church. He stresses its unity (v. 5), its diversity (v. 6), and the need to recognize one’s gift and to use it eagerly and appropriately in service to others (vv. 6–8).

To prophesy is, at its root, to speak the Word of God via the inspiration and calling of the Holy Spirit. In this sense, NT prophecy is identical to OT prophecy. Prophecy is distinguished here and elsewhere from teaching (v. 7; cf. Acts 13:1; 1 Cor. 12:29; Eph. 4:11) because it is a revelatory gift (Acts 13:1–3; 21:10, 11).

**in proportion to our faith.** Some `interpreters see “faith” as the prophet’s own faith (cf. vv. 3, 6). Less plausibly, others understand “faith” to mean the truth content of the gospel as the standard and measure of each prophetic utterance (referred to in theology as “the analogy of faith”), a vital criterion for testing whether the utterance conforms to “the pattern of the sound words” (2 Tim. 1:13).

Paul recognizes the wide variety and practicality of these gifts (Gk. _charismata_) and the intertwining of natural endowments with them. Throughout this passage, it is clear that the blessing of those who are ministered to is the paramount consideration in using the gifts., 8

As in 1 Cor. 12; 13, when discussing the church as the body of Christ, Paul stresses the importance of love. His series of rapid exhortations carries echoes of Jesus’ teaching and is expressed in vivid language.

**12:9 be genuine.** In classical Greek drama, the _hypokrit?s_ (actor) wore a face-mask. The Christian’s loving behavior should not be playing a part or wearing a mask, but an authentic expression of goodwill.

verse_quote: Love one another with brotherly affection.
note: An unusual linguistic combination of brotherly love with the love of natural affection. The church is a family, the “household of God” (1 Tim. 3:15; cf. 1 Tim. 5:1, 2).

There must be no hesitation or sloth in Christian living. The Christian should be “fervent,” living for Christ with enthusiasm and energy. The text note here and in Acts 18:25, where the same expression occurs, is probably correct to suggest that God’s Spirit evokes and empowers believers’ fervent eagerness to serve the Lord and His people.

Generosity toward believers in need distinguished the early believers’ fellowship (Acts 2:42, 44–46; 4:32–37; Heb. 6:10; 13:16).

**hospitality.** Hospitality for visiting Christians was another important part of early Christian life (Heb. 13:2; 3 John 5–8).
See Luke 6:27, 28.
See Luke 6:31. The genuine unity of the body of Christ is especially evident in the empathy of its members in moments of high joy or deep sorrow.

Paul’s language gives the idea of Christians’ sharing the same thoughts with respect to one another, another indication of the strategic role of the mind in sanctification (vv. 1, 2). One manifestation of this will be an absence of conceit and pride in worldly position (Phil. 2:1–8). Christians should be distinguished by their readiness to “associate with the lowly.”

**Never be wise in your own sight.** See Prov. 3:7. A further focus on the thought-world. How we think determines how we live.
The unifying theme in vv. 17–21 is the way the Christian reacts to the non-Christian environment.

The Christian is a peacemaker by obligation and aim. Harmony is not always possible, since truth divides as well as unites. Paul’s double qualification (“If ... so far as”) recognizes this, but the obligation to strive for peace in personal relations with others remains.

The Christian must be free from the desire to “get even.” Such release from the instinct for revenge is possible because the believer knows that God will right all wrongs in His own perfect judgment (Deut. 32:35). Moreover, Scripture urges us to show grace to the wrongdoer because God is patient with him (Prov. 25:21, 22).

verse_quote: heap burning coals on his head.
note: Doing good to an enemy may lead to his conscience’s being pricked, and thus to his conversion, or it could at least lead to such a sense of shame that evil behavior is modified.

Christians have a distinct rationale for appropriate submission to the governing authorities: the recognition that God Himself is the source of government in society (Prov. 8:15, 16; Dan. 2:21). See theological note “Civil Government” on next page.
Rebellion against civil authority implies rebellion against God’s ordinance (Ex. 22:28)., 3

The state’s authority is for the benefit of the governed, the defense of the innocent, and the restraint of evil behavior. These are its normal and divinely ordained functions, and Paul assumes that they may be realized in practical terms even when governments are professedly non-Christian. The NT also demonstrates, realistically, that human governments are quite capable of abusing justice (Rev. 13).

**the sword.** The exercise of force by the civil magistrate (cf. 1 Pet. 2:13, 14). This power is given by God and must be used according to God’s will. The civil magistrate may lawfully engage in defensive wars against aggression (cf. Deut. 20; 1 Chr. 5:22; Eccl. 3:8). The civil magistrate may also lawfully carry out capital punishment under specific conditions (cf. Gen. 9:6; Deut. 17:6, 7). Elsewhere Paul accepts the principle of such punishment where appropriate (Acts 25:11).

**wrath.** What the individual must not do out of a motive of revenge (12:19), the state, as God’s servant with a distinctive calling, may legitimately do in the pursuit of justice.

Christian submission is a response of the conscience as it is instructed by divine revelation. Because the task of government is divinely ordained and requires financial support, the Christian must pay taxes with a distinctive motive and understanding, as an element of obedience and devotion to God (Matt. 17:24–27; 22:15–21).

verse_quote: Pay to all what is owed to them.
note: See Matt. 22:21. Paul is evidently familiar with Jesus’ statement to “render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s,” and here indicates how it is applied. On “honor,” see 1 Pet. 2:17; Acts 23:2–5.

Paul now further applies his basic principle of Christian consecration. The connecting link between vv. 7 and 8 is found in the exhortation of v. 7 that the Christian has a financial obligation to the state. This is an application of a general principle now stated, that all obligations must be met. One obligation is permanent—to love others.

**13:8 has fulfilled the law.** See theological note “Antinomianism” on p. 2272. Since the law of God is the law of love (Matt. 22:38–40) and love of God and love of neighbor summarize our moral obligation, then truly loving one’s neighbor (vv. 8, 9), or keeping the second table of the law, “fulfills” God’s requirements (v. 10). Those who do not rely on their own law-keeping but on God’s work in Christ are now empowered by His Spirit to progressively fulfill the law’s righteous requirement (8:1–4).

See Lev. 19:18; theological note “Love” on p. 2036. This is not an encouragement to self-love, but rather a summons to extend to others the concern that we so naturally express in protecting and providing for ourselves (Luke 6:31).

Spiritual discernment is rooted in the apprehension of divine revelation. Paul’s stress on the role of the mind is again evident. Paul wants the believer to live in the light of the return of Christ.

**salvation.** Here in the sense of future, final redemption (5:9, 10; 8:23; 1 Thess. 5:9).

Paul speaks here of the “night” of this present age. The “light of the world” has come (John 8:12), and we must prepare for the second advent of Christ and the consummation of the age to come.

**let us cast off ... put on.** The use of the metaphor “armor of light” stresses that developing positive spiritual graces, not merely rejecting vices, is essential to spiritual defense. Elsewhere, Paul lists pieces of this “armor” in contexts that similarly contrast daylight to night’s darkness (1 Thess. 5:4–8; Eph. 6:10–20).

This passage played a crucial role in the conversion of Augustine of Hippo. Augustine wrote in his _Confessions_ that upon reading these verses, “It was as though the light of confidence flooded my heart and all the darkness of doubt was dispelled.”

**13:13 Let us walk properly.** Paul’s warning against a sinful lifestyle strikingly includes not only the traditional sins of the body (“orgies and drunkenness ... sexual immorality and sensuality”) but also insidious vices or practices that can be harbored in the heart or even paraded in the church (“quarreling and jealousy”).

**13:14 But put on the Lord Jesus Christ.** A further exposition of what it means to “put on the armor of light” (v. 12), showing that those who are in Christ must live consistently with their new identity in union with Christ (Eph. 4:1).

verse_quote: As for the one who is weak.
note:
Paul now turns to address a specific application of the law of love to the Roman Christians. The Christian’s basic attitude toward a fellow Christian is one of welcome and acceptance based on God’s attitude to us in Christ (v. 3; 15:7). There must be charity toward the “weak” person whose conscience is still bound by scruples from which the gospel normally sets us free (v. 2). But those whose consciences still require them to abstain from meat (which is not in itself sinful) must refrain from condemning those who can consume it with a clear conscience (v. 3). Both “weak” and “strong” with respect to diet or calendar (vv. 5, 6) must welcome the other in deference to their common Lord, to whom each ultimately answers.

**quarrel over opinions.** In this instance, questions of food, drink, and the religious observation of days. While Paul does not regard these controversies as insoluble, he regards the unity of the church’s fellowship as more important than resolving them to everyone’s satisfaction (cf. 12:5, 10, 16). The issues in view here do not belong to the gospel, but to the relative strength or weakness of the individual’s faith in the gospel. Where essentials of the gospel are at stake, Paul’s response is very different (e.g., Gal. 1:6, 7; 3:1–5; Phil. 3:2, 18, 19).

Vegetarianism is not required by the OT, though it appears there (e.g., Dan. 1:12). Possibly some in Rome have embraced a vegetarian diet to circumvent the issues of conscience surrounding the association of meat with pagan temple rituals (1 Cor. 8–10).

The tendency of those who better understand the gospel is to be impatient with the inhibitions of the “weak” as legalistic bondage. The temptation of the “weak” is to condemn the “strong” for behavior that seems to be lawless license. These mistaken responses should yield to the light of God’s gracious acceptance of both “weak” and “strong.” Furthermore, a fellow believer is God’s servant, not ours, and is answerable to Him, not to us. It must be understood that the issues in such possible disputes are not matters of real morality, but of morally indifferent things.

verse_quote: One person esteems one day as better than another.
note:
A pattern of holy days characterizes the Jewish year, and it is to these days that Paul refers, and not the weekly Sabbath. If the Sabbath were in view it would have been more natural to say, “One man considers the Sabbath above the other days.”

**Each one should be fully convinced.** See 4:21 for another instance of this term. It is spiritually perilous to act contrary to one’s conscience even if the conscience is weak and forbids what God Himself permits (vv. 14, 15; 1 Cor. 8:9–13).

An appeal to what is shared by both groups (v. 3), namely, the desire to honor the same Lord. That both belong to Him puts minor divisions into perspective. See theological note “The Kingdom of God” on p. 1823., 7

Christ alone is the Lord (v. 8) and Judge of His people. The cost to Him of this privilege was immense and exposes the inappropriateness of believers’ judging or despising their brothers. We must give an account of our own lives to the Lord, as those being judged, not as those who judge.

While Paul’s own conscience has been liberated by the teaching of Christ (v. 14; cf. Mark 7:18, 19) he recognizes that not all believers have come to enjoy such freedom. Consideration for such brethren (“walking in love,” v. 15) means avoiding behavior that might distress them. Two specific injunctions to this effect follow in vv. 15, 16.

While Paul counsels stronger believers to be sensitive to the consciences of weaker believers, this statement, which the entire church will read, indirectly calls the weak believers to mature in the faith and understand that they are free in Christ to partake of His good gifts. Because nothing is unclean in itself, they may not exercise the “tyranny of the weaker brother” and impose their personal scruples regarding indifferent matters on other believers.

verse_quote: By what you eat, do not destroy the one for whom Christ died.
note: In the context of Jewish faith, “destroy” means to cut off from the covenant community (Deut. 28:21, 45, 48, 51, 61, 63). To encourage behavior that weak believers’ consciences forbid is to encourage them to go against their conscience, a serious and dangerous act.

The strong are urged to weigh the importance of exercising their freedom against two considerations: (a) the use of their freedom may bring division and disrepute on the church; (b) God’s kingdom (and therefore our freedom) is not a matter of food and drink, but of the blessings of grace (5:1, 2). Since freedom does not consist in these things, it cannot be lost by our refraining from them.
See v. 16. While God alone is our Judge (v. 12), the impact of our actions on others plays a vital role in fellowship and evangelism.

The believer’s responsibility is now stated positively: avoiding the destruction of others is complemented by promoting “peace” and the things that “upbuild” (v. 19). For the “strong” (15:1), this includes both maintaining fellowship with the “weak” and also encouraging them to understand the liberty that is theirs in Christ. When such aims are in view, freedom to eat and drink will be made subordinate; the well-being of the brother will take precedence over the enjoyment of meat and wine.
Paul further urges the “strong” (15:1) to enjoy the fact of their liberty of conscience in God’s presence (while refraining from publicly exercising it)., 23

verse_quote: We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak.
note: Paul considers himself one of the “strong.” He sees the misinformed conscience of the “weak” as real weakness, yet he emphasizes the responsibility of the “strong” to be patient with the “weak.” He does not encourage feelings of pride, or flaunting one’s freedom in matters offensive to the weak.

. Paul will never modify the gospel for the sake of pleasing people (Gal. 1:10), but he is ready to forgo exercise of his liberty in Christ in order to serve and spiritually safeguard others. See 14:19; cf. 1 Cor. 8:1; 10:23, 24, 32, 33.

Paul quotes from Ps. 69, one of the most frequently quoted psalms in the NT (see 11:9–10; John 2:17; Acts 1:20). The willingness of the Messiah to deny Himself and suffer for the benefit of others should serve as an example to the Christians in Rome.
It is basic NT teaching that the OT Scriptures were written by divine inspiration for the benefit of Christians (1 Cor. 10:11; 2 Tim. 3:15–17; 1 Pet. 1:10–12).

See 10:9, 10. Unity in the church is essential if God is to be glorified. Paul has demonstrated that humanity has fallen short of God’s glory but is restored to it in Christ’s reconciling work (1:21, 23; 3:23; 5:2, 11; 8:17, 30).

verse_quote: Christ ... a servant to the circumcised.
note:
The mutual acceptance of believers is rooted in Christ’s humility (Mark 10:45). The ministry of Jesus the Messiah first of all to the lost sheep of Israel (Matt. 15:24)—“to the Jew first” (1:16)—confirms God’s truthfulness in His fidelity to His promises, as Paul demonstrated at length in chs. 9–11.

**15:9 the Gentiles.** God’s faithfulness in drawing a remnant of Israelites to faith in Christ gives Gentile believers reason to rely on His faithful Word, while the Gentiles’ inclusion shows Jewish and Gentile believers alike that God keeps His promises not because He is indebted to His creatures but because of His mercy and faithfulness (see 11:30–32).

A series of quotations from three sections of the Hebrew Scriptures—the Law (v. 10, Deut. 32:43 LXX), the Prophets (v. 12, Is. 11:10), and the Writings (vv. 9, 11, Pss. 18:49; 117:1)—represents the unanimous testimony of the entire OT to God’s intention to include the Gentiles with His people Israel in His worship and under His reign.

See theological note “Hope” on p. 2206. What was described as the effect of Scripture in v. 4 (having hope) and promised in the citation from Is. 11:10 (v. 12) is now attributed to the work of the Holy Spirit. Paul here follows a pattern evident throughout the NT: God’s saving acts are attributed to God’s Word as well as to the work of the Holy Spirit (e.g., regeneration, 1 Pet. 1:23; sanctification, John 17:17; salvation, Rom. 1:16; searching the heart, Heb. 4:12).

Paul now begins to draw his letter to a close by returning to the theme of its introduction—his own ministry and his vision for the expansion of the influence of the gospel.

**15:14 my brothers.** A further indication of deeply felt emotion (1:13; 7:1, 4; 11:25; 12:1). Paul graciously assures the Romans that his lengthy exposition of the gospel is not intended to raise doubts about their spiritual understanding. Their knowledge of the gospel and ability to apply it practically in mutual admonition (“able to instruct one another”; cf. Col. 3:16) is not in question.

verse_quote: a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles.
note:
Although Paul has not yet reached Rome, the largely Gentile composition of the congregations in the imperial capital brings these believers under his distinctive sphere of authority as apostle to the Gentiles (11:13; Gal. 2:7–9).

**priestly service of the gospel of God.** Paul sees the preaching of the gospel as the means by which the Gentiles will be brought to God as a sacrificial thank offering (12:1). For similar uses of priestly sacrificial imagery, see Phil. 2:17; 4:18; Heb. 13:15, 16.
Paul describes his ministry very naturally in Trinitarian terms (God the Father, vv. 17, 18; God the Son, vv. 17–20; God the Holy Spirit, v. 19; cf. v. 16).

See Ex. 7:3; Deut. 4:34; 6:22; 7:19; Is. 8:18; Dan. 6:27. A phrase rooted in the authentication of Moses’ ministry at the time of the exodus. God periodically gave such miracles at critical junctures of redemptive history, such as the exodus, the prophetic ministries of Elijah and Elisha, the preserving of His people in the time of Daniel, and the ministry of Christ and the apostles. These events are unusual rather than normal and point to the successive stages of redemptive history and the new revelation that accompanied them. As signs and wonders expressed God’s endorsement of Jesus’ ministry and claims (Acts 2:22–24; John 5:36), so Paul can invoke such signs as authenticating his own apostolic authority (2 Cor. 12:12; cf. Heb. 2:3, 4).

**from Jerusalem and all the way around to Illyricum.** Paul’s journeys, according to Acts, stretched from the eastern Mediterranean as far west as Macedonia. There is no biblical record of his personally entering Illyricum (northwest of Macedonia). While he may have done so, it seems more likely that he means he went as far as Macedonia. He established centers of mission, rather than preaching personally in every village. From such centers, even Illyricum may have been reached with the gospel.
Paul’s call is to focus on laying the foundation of the knowledge of Christ in communities where the gospel is unknown (1 Cor. 3:10, 11).

Two things now make the visit to Rome possible: (a) the present phase of Paul’s commission has been fulfilled (he has “no ... room” to preach in the eastern Mediterranean because Christ’s name has reached those region’s urban centers, v. 20); (b) the new phase involving outreach to Spain is imminent, and Paul seeks their partnership in it.

**15:24 Spain.** The western extremity of the ancient world. Some suggest Paul thought of Spain as the Tarshish of Is. 66:19, and saw the extension of his preaching there as significant for the Christian mission (Matt. 24:14; Acts 1:8).

Paul now discloses his immediate plans to visit Jerusalem with the gifts the Gentile churches raised for the Christians there (see 2 Cor. 8; 9). In this era, Jerusalem is an impoverished city in general; but additionally, the Christians there are suffering particular hardship as a suspect minority. But Paul sees a significance deeper than charity in the gift. It is a duty (v. 27), a solemn obligation of the Gentiles in view of the privilege they have received in being grafted into God’s olive tree (11:17), coming to share in Israel’s covenant relation to God through the gospel with its spiritual blessings. This reciprocity conforms to the general principle that those who receive spiritual blessings should share their own material blessings (1 Cor. 9:3–14; Gal. 6:6).

verse_quote: fullness of the blessing of Christ.
note: A striking comment in view of the manner in which Paul’s aspirations are ultimately fulfilled, namely, in imperial custody (Acts 28:11–16) and facing unspecified charges that can, in principle, lead to execution (Phil. 1:19–21).

Paul’s concern is twofold: (a) that he will be protected from the hostility of the unbelieving Jews that has pursued him for so much of the whole of his ministry (see Acts 21:27–22:39; 23:12–35); (b) that Jewish Christians in Jerusalem will respond favorably to the Gentile gift, and therefore to the apostle’s ministry (v. 32; see Acts 21:17–20).
One of Paul’s favorite designations for God (16:20; 2 Cor. 13:11; Phil. 4:9; 1 Thess. 5:23; 2 Thess. 3:16), but particularly appropriate here in regard to his present struggle (v. 30).

Paul’s letters typically end with personal news and greetings. The closing chapter of Romans is remarkable for the large number of fellow believers mentioned. These verses give an insight into the warmth of the apostle’s personal relationships as well as the fellowship of the early Christians. These greetings are especially noteworthy when we consider that Paul has not personally visited the church at Rome. He names so many among the believers at Rome to demonstrate his many personal ties with the congregations that make up this church in the imperial capital.

**16:1 Phoebe.** Probably the bearer of Paul’s letter. The name is common in Greek mythology and indicates a Gentile background.

**a servant.** Paul’s word (Gk. _diakonos_) is variously translated as “servant” (1 Tim. 4:6), or “deacon” (Phil. 1:1; 1 Tim. 3:8). It is unlikely Paul uses the term to refer to the specific church office of deacon; he is instead describing Phoebe as a servant of the church in a more general sense.

**Cenchreae.** The port of Corinth on the Saronic Gulf, indicating Paul’s location when Romans was sent.

The couple were tentmakers like Paul (Acts 18:3). He was with them in Corinth. They had left Rome after the decree of Claudius and accompanied Paul to Ephesus (Acts 18:18). They taught Apollos (Acts 18:24–26) and later returned to Rome.
Evidently the first of a harvest of converts in the Roman province of Asia.

verse_quote: Mary, who has worked hard for you.
note: Paul recognizes the devoted service of women (v. 12).

Early commentators understood these to be a husband and wife. They were fellow Jews, and had been converted (“in Christ”) before Paul himself. They had apparently been in prison at some time with Paul (cf. 2 Cor. 11:23) and had served with distinction.

**well known to the apostles.** Some translate this as “outstanding among the apostles” (e.g., NIV) and use these words to justify women’s ordination, though the ESV’s rendering is the better translation. Either way, it must be recalled that the word “apostle” is used not only in a technical sense for the Twelve and Paul, but in a nontechnical sense as well, referring to church envoys (text note; 2 Cor. 1:1 note). Paul is elsewhere clear that only men may be ordained to the office of “overseer,” i.e., elder. (1 Tim. 3:1–7)
Probably a slave, whose name appears on a tomb in the Catacomb of Domitilla, niece of the Emperor Domitian.
Common slave names, the former Roman, the latter Greek.

A common Greek name. It is likely that Paul declares him “approved in Christ” because he had distinguished himself through trial and remained faithful.

**Aristobulus.** This may be the grandson of Herod the Great and friend of the Emperor Claudius.

Perhaps a freedman of the household of Herod, since freedmen took the name of their patron.

**Narcissus.** Perhaps to be identified with Narcissus, the aide of Claudius, who was forced to commit suicide by Agrippina after Nero’s accession.

Two women with names from a common root (“gentle,” “delicate”) and who were therefore possibly sisters.

**Persis.** Another woman, recognized for her diligent work for the Lord.

One of the most intriguing of the names listed in view of Mark 15:21, a gospel possibly written from Rome. “Chosen” may reflect the unique circumstances that brought his family into contact with Christ. Simeon of Cyrene, whom soldiers compelled to carry Jesus’ crossbeam to the place of execution, had two sons, Alexander and Rufus, who were presumably known to Mark’s readers. The Rufus whom the apostle mentions here may be the same Rufus who was the son of Simon. Paul’s allusion to the mother as “his mother ... to me as well” suggests deep affection for the family.

The kiss remains a common token of greeting in the East even to this day. Here and elsewhere, Paul urges the believers to sanctify their greetings as symbols of Christian fellowship (1 Cor. 16:20; 2 Cor. 13:12; 1 Thess. 5:26), and the practice was also enjoined by Peter for the churches of Asia Minor (1 Pet. 5:14).

Reflection on his knowledge of these believers, their problems in Rome (ch. 14), and the divisive activity of Satan (v. 20) evokes an urgent summons for Christians to guard their unity (Eph. 4:3). They are to avoid those “who cause divisions ... contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught.” Bluntly, he indicates that their divisive spirit is sinful, a mark of life in the flesh, and a form of self-indulgence (Gal. 5:19, 20). Christians must learn not to be deceived by “smooth talk and flattery” (v. 18).

verse_quote: your obedience is known to all.
note:
Not surprisingly, the faith of Jesus’ followers living in the capital of the vast Roman Empire (1:8) and the obedience that flowed from that faith have become well known throughout the Greco-Roman world.

**innocent.** The Romans need spiritual wisdom and hearts without any taint of evil.

Prior to the closing greetings and doxology, Paul includes a promise of a prophetic nature, rooted in the first biblical deliverance promise in Gen. 3:15 (see Ps. 91:13; Luke 10:18, 19). Satan stands behind what is “evil” (v. 19; cf. Gen. 3:12; see also theological note “Satan” on p. 760). “The God of peace” (wholeness and integrity as well as tranquility) will act as the divine warrior to overcome him. This will take place “soon.” Paul is speaking here about the last things, which by faith are always seen as near at hand.

**The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.** A characteristically Pauline ending (Gal. 6:18; 1 Thess. 5:28).

Along with Silas, Timothy was Paul’s closest coworker after the disagreement with Barnabas (Acts 15:36–40) and is mentioned in ten of Paul’s letters. Lucius (whom some identify with Luke), Jason (possibly Paul’s host in Thessalonica, Acts 17:5–9), and Sosipater (Acts 20:4) were possibly church delegates accompanying Paul to deliver the collection in Jerusalem.
Paul regularly used a secretary, identifying his letters as his own by a brief greeting written in his own handwriting (1 Cor. 16:21; Gal. 6:11; Col. 4:18; 2 Thess. 3:17).

Paul may have been residing with Gaius at the time of writing. He is presumably to be identified with the Gaius of 1 Cor. 1:14, and may be the (Gaius?) Titius Justus of Acts 18:7. An Erastus is mentioned in Acts 19:22 and 2 Tim. 4:20. We do not know whether this is the same man. Of greater interest is that a Christian held a post of such responsibility in the local government of Corinth, a fact that illustrates that the earliest Christians could and did render faithful service in governmental positions (see 13:1–7). Of Quartus nothing is known.

The authenticity of this closing doxology is questioned by some on the grounds of its length, its emphasis on mystery, and its textual history (it is found at different points in the letter, or even omitted altogether in various ancient manuscripts). There is, however, a certain appropriateness about its length, coming at the end of a letter like Romans. Its themes draw to a fitting conclusion much that has already been said. In particular, Paul draws attention to his own teaching of the gospel (2:16; cf. 1 Thess. 1:5; 2 Tim. 2:8) and its power to edify (1:11), to the revelation of God’s mystery (11:25; cf. Eph. 3:2–6), to faith and obedience among the nations (1:5), and to the wisdom of God in redemption (11:33; cf. Eph. 3:10–12).

verse_quote: but has now ... through the prophetic writings has been made known.
note: Paul’s “now” might suggest that he is referring to the NT Scriptures, but his emphasis is that it is only now that the message already enshrined in the OT and “now” “disclosed” in the light of Christ’s coming is spread to the nations, as he noted earlier in 1:2 and 3:21.
